title: Vector Databases
subtitle: 30 questions covering all key topics · Shuffled each attempt

questions.q: What is a vector (embedding) in the context of vector databases?
opts: A compressed binary representation of a file
An array of numbers that represents an object, where similar objects have similar vectors
A hash value used to uniquely identify a document
A pointer to a row in a traditional relational database
questions.expl: A vector (or embedding) is an array of numbers representing something — a word, image, user, or product. The magic is that similar things end up with similar vectors, reflecting semantic relationships geometrically.

questions.q: Typical embedding dimensions range from 128 to 1536. How much raw memory does a single 1536-dimension float32 vector consume?
opts: About 600 bytes
About 6KB
About 60KB
About 600KB
questions.expl: Each float32 dimension is 4 bytes. 1536 × 4 = 6,144 bytes ≈ 6KB. This is bigger than most people expect, and it adds up fast — 1 million vectors is ~6GB before index overhead.

questions.q: Why can't traditional databases answer 'find me documents similar to this one' efficiently?
opts: Traditional databases don't support floating point numbers
Traditional databases are great at exact lookups but have no native concept of similarity search
Traditional databases compress data too aggressively for similarity comparisons
Traditional databases lack support for arrays as column types
questions.expl: Traditional databases excel at exact lookups (give me user ID 12345) but have no native mechanism for similarity search across high-dimensional vectors. That's the core problem vector databases solve.

questions.q: What does 'recall' mean in the context of Approximate Nearest Neighbor search?
opts: The fraction of queries that return in under 10ms
Of the true top-K nearest neighbors, the fraction that the ANN search actually found
The percentage of vectors that fit into RAM
The accuracy of the embedding model on a test set
questions.expl: Recall measures ANN quality: of the true top-K nearest neighbors, what fraction did we actually find? A recall of 0.95 means we found 95% of the true nearest neighbors — usually good enough for real applications.

questions.q: What are the three core tradeoffs that every vector database forces you to balance?
opts: Cost, correctness, and complexity
Recall, latency, and memory
Throughput, durability, and consistency
Indexing time, query time, and storage
questions.expl: Every vector database design involves smooth tradeoffs between recall (how accurate are results?), latency (how fast can we return results?), and memory (how much space does the index consume, especially RAM?).

questions.q: Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors and ignores magnitude. When is this particularly useful?
opts: When vectors have very different numbers of dimensions
When embeddings are normalized, which most embedding models produce
When comparing binary vectors using bitwise operations
When computing similarity between integers rather than floats
questions.expl: Cosine similarity is ideal when embeddings are normalized (magnitude = 1), which most embedding models produce. It measures direction alone, so two vectors pointing the same way score 1.0 regardless of their lengths.

questions.q: Which similarity metric is most naturally suited to Locality Sensitive Hashing using random hyperplanes?
opts: Euclidean (L2) distance
Dot product
Cosine similarity
Hamming distance
questions.expl: Random hyperplane LSH works by checking which side of a hyperplane a vector falls on — this directly corresponds to cosine similarity. Vectors at a small angle share most hyperplane sides, producing similar hashes.

questions.q: What is the key difference between dot product and cosine similarity?
opts: Dot product only works for 2D vectors
Cosine similarity measures direction only; dot product also incorporates the magnitudes of both vectors
Dot product requires binary vectors; cosine works on floats
Cosine similarity is always faster to compute than dot product
questions.expl: Cosine similarity normalizes for magnitude, measuring only the angle between vectors. Dot product = cosine similarity × (magnitude of A) × (magnitude of B). Some systems use dot product because it's slightly faster to compute.

questions.q: HNSW's design is analogous to which classical data structure?
opts: B-trees
Bloom filters
Skip lists
Hash maps
questions.expl: HNSW applies the same idea as skip lists: add 'express lane' layers above a base structure. Skip lists have O(log n) search by jumping over elements at higher layers — HNSW does the same in high-dimensional vector space.

questions.q: When searching an HNSW index, what is the correct traversal order?
opts: Start at the densest bottom layer (Layer 0) and work upward
Start at the sparse top layer, greedily navigate toward the query, drop to denser layers, finish with a local search at Layer 0
Start at a random node in Layer 0 and do breadth-first search
Query all layers simultaneously and merge results
questions.expl: HNSW search starts at a sparse top layer, greedily moves toward the target, drops to progressively denser layers, and does a thorough local search at Layer 0 where all vectors live. Top layers 'zoom in' to the right region quickly.

questions.q: What is the main memory cost drawback of HNSW compared to simpler indexes?
opts: HNSW requires storing all vectors in GPU memory
HNSW must store the graph structure (edges) on top of the raw vectors, roughly doubling memory usage
HNSW compresses vectors, requiring decompression at query time
HNSW needs a separate machine for each layer of the graph
questions.expl: HNSW stores a multi-layer graph where each vector is a node with edges to its nearest neighbors. This graph structure roughly doubles the memory required compared to storing raw vectors alone.

questions.q: What happens to HNSW graph quality over time with many inserts?
opts: Nothing — HNSW is fully self-balancing like a red-black tree
Graph structure can degrade since new vectors may not be as well-connected as those present during initial build
HNSW automatically promotes the most-connected vectors to higher layers
Insert order has no effect on HNSW quality
questions.expl: New vectors inserted into HNSW find their place and establish connections, but they may not integrate as well as vectors present during the initial build. Over time, graph quality can degrade, which is one reason for periodic index rebuilds.

questions.q: What is the core idea behind IVF (Inverted File Index) for vector search?
opts: It builds a multi-layer graph like HNSW but using inverted edges
It partitions vectors into clusters using k-means; at query time only the closest clusters are searched
It hashes vectors so similar vectors collide in the same bucket
It stores vectors as a binary tree sorted by magnitude
questions.expl: IVF clusters vectors using k-means, each cluster with a centroid. At query time, you find the closest centroids then search only within those clusters — potentially skipping 99%+ of comparisons.

questions.q: In IVF, what does the parameter 'nprobe' control?
opts: The number of dimensions in the embedding
How many clusters are searched at query time — higher nprobe means better recall but slower queries
The number of k-means iterations during index build
The maximum number of results returned per query
questions.expl: nprobe controls how many clusters are searched at query time. Higher nprobe → more clusters searched → better recall but higher latency. It's the key tuning knob for the recall/latency tradeoff in IVF.

questions.q: How does LSH (Locality Sensitive Hashing) differ fundamentally from regular hash functions?
opts: LSH uses cryptographic hashing for security; regular hashes don't
Regular hash functions try to avoid collisions; LSH is designed so similar items are likely to collide in the same bucket
LSH only works for integer vectors; regular hashing works for any type
LSH stores vectors in sorted order; regular hashing uses random ordering
questions.expl: Regular hash functions avoid collisions to distribute items evenly. LSH deliberately causes collisions for similar items — vectors that are geometrically close hash to the same bucket, enabling fast similarity search.

questions.q: What is Annoy's killer feature that made it popular at companies like Spotify?
opts: It achieves higher recall than HNSW on all datasets
Its indexes can be memory-mapped (mmap'd), allowing multiple processes to share an index and work with indexes larger than RAM
It supports real-time inserts without index rebuilds
It automatically selects the optimal number of trees based on dataset size
questions.expl: Annoy stores its entire index as a single file that can be mmap'd into memory. This means multiple processes share the same index without copying, indexes can exceed RAM size, and loading is instant.

questions.q: What is Annoy's critical limitation that makes it unsuitable for real-time applications?
opts: Annoy only supports cosine similarity, not Euclidean distance
Annoy indexes are immutable — you cannot add or remove vectors without rebuilding the entire index
Annoy requires GPU acceleration for acceptable query latency
Annoy only works with embeddings of 128 dimensions or fewer
questions.expl: Once built, an Annoy index cannot be modified. Adding or removing a single vector requires rebuilding the entire index from scratch. This makes it great for static datasets but unsuitable for real-time writes.

questions.q: What is the key risk of post-filtering in vector search?
opts: Post-filtering always returns too many results, causing high latency
If the filter is very restrictive, you may not find K results after filtering the top-N vector results
Post-filtering is incompatible with HNSW indexes
Post-filtering requires re-ranking all results from scratch
questions.expl: Post-filtering finds top-N similar vectors then applies the filter. If the filter is very restrictive (e.g., in-stock items < 1% of catalog), you may not find K results in your top-N. You can increase N but that means more work.

questions.q: How does Pinecone handle metadata filtering differently from pgvector?
opts: Pinecone relies on the query planner to choose between the vector index and B-tree index
Pinecone applies filters during ANN search by intersecting metadata inverted indexes with vector search in a single operation
Pinecone only supports post-filtering for performance reasons
Pinecone converts all metadata to vectors and does a secondary vector search
questions.expl: Pinecone maintains inverted indexes on metadata fields alongside the vector index and intersects them during ANN search — not before or after. This makes filtering a first-class operation rather than a tacked-on step.

questions.q: What is 'hybrid search' in the context of vector databases?
opts: Combining HNSW and IVF indexes for the same query
Running both full-text keyword search and vector similarity search simultaneously and merging the results
Using both CPU and GPU to accelerate a single vector search query
Searching across multiple vector databases and deduplicating results
questions.expl: Hybrid search combines full-text keyword matching with vector similarity search. A query like 'red running shoes' might use keyword matching for 'red' while using vector similarity for semantic relevance — often giving better results than either alone.

questions.q: Why are vector database updates typically more expensive than updates in traditional databases?
opts: Vector DBs must re-train the embedding model on every update
Updating a vector in HNSW means finding its place in a multi-layer graph and updating connections at each layer, not just modifying a row
Vector DBs store data on slower disk tiers by default
Vector DBs must re-cluster all vectors using k-means after every insert
questions.expl: Traditional DBs handle updates in real-time because they're designed for it. In HNSW, each new vector must find its place in a multi-layer graph and establish connections — expensive at scale, and graph quality can degrade with many inserts.

questions.q: What is the 'hot and cold index' pattern used for in vector databases?
opts: Hot index stores frequently accessed vectors in GPU memory; cold index is on disk
A small hot index holds recent inserts for immediate searchability; a large cold index holds older data. Queries search both. Periodically, hot is merged into cold with a full rebuild.
Hot index uses HNSW; cold index uses IVF for faster rebuilds
Hot index stores high-similarity vectors; cold index stores low-similarity ones
questions.expl: Because inserting into a large HNSW index is expensive, many systems maintain a small hot index (even just a flat list) for recent inserts and a large optimized cold index for older data. Queries search both and merge. The hot index is periodically rebuilt into the cold index.

questions.q: How are deletions typically handled in vector databases?
opts: Vectors are immediately removed from the HNSW graph and connections are re-wired
Most systems use soft deletes — marking vectors as deleted — rather than actually removing them, until a rebuild or compaction
Deletions are queued and applied during nightly batch jobs only
Deleted vectors are moved to a cold index and excluded from queries automatically
questions.expl: Most vector DBs use soft deletes: mark the vector as deleted rather than actually removing it from the index. This means deleted vectors still consume space and can slow queries until you rebuild or compact the index.

questions.q: What is the article's primary recommendation for getting started with vector search?
opts: Always use a purpose-built vector DB like Pinecone from day one for production readiness
Start with extensions to databases you're already using (pgvector, ES kNN, Redis Vector Search) before reaching for a dedicated vector DB
Build your own HNSW implementation to understand the internals before using a third-party solution
Start with Chroma for prototyping and migrate directly to Milvus for production
questions.expl: The article explicitly says 'start simple.' Extensions like pgvector handle millions of vectors and avoid operational overhead of another system. Only reach for a dedicated vector DB when scale or features demand it.

questions.q: At roughly what scale should you consider migrating to a purpose-built vector database?
opts: More than 1 million vectors
More than 10 million vectors
More than 100 million vectors
More than 1 billion vectors
questions.expl: The article's rule of thumb: if you're dealing with more than 100 million vectors, consider a purpose-built vector database. Below that, extensions to existing databases typically handle the load without the operational overhead.

questions.q: Which purpose-built vector database is described as fully managed and serverless?
opts: Milvus
Weaviate
Qdrant
Pinecone
questions.expl: Pinecone is fully managed and serverless. You just call an API — no infrastructure to run. The trade-off is cost and less control compared to self-hosted options like Milvus, Weaviate, or Qdrant.

questions.q: What is a RAG system and how does a vector database fit in?
opts: RAG systems use vector databases as the primary source of truth, replacing traditional databases entirely
Vector search retrieves relevant documents from a knowledge base, which are then passed as context to an LLM to synthesize an answer
RAG uses the vector database to store LLM responses for caching and deduplication
RAG trains a new embedding model for each query using the vector database as training data
questions.expl: In RAG, a user query is embedded and used to search the vector database for relevant documents. Those documents are passed as context to an LLM which synthesizes an answer. The vector DB enables the LLM to 'know' about custom or recent data.

questions.q: In a two-stage retrieval architecture, what role does the vector database play?
opts: The vector database is the final ranker, producing the exact top-K results served to users
The vector database acts as a fast candidate generator (e.g., top 1000), and a more sophisticated model reranks the candidates to produce the final results
The vector database handles keyword search while a separate model handles semantic search
The vector database stores user feedback used to retrain the embedding model
questions.expl: In two-stage retrieval, the vector database is the lightweight first stage — fast but approximate, returning a large candidate set (maybe top 1000). A slower, more powerful reranker then refines these to produce the final results. Common in recommendation systems.

questions.q: What is 'embedding drift' and why is it operationally challenging?
opts: Embedding drift is when vectors gradually move toward zero due to floating point rounding
When you update your embedding model, old embeddings are incompatible with new ones — requiring re-embedding everything or running multiple indexes during transition
Embedding drift refers to clusters shifting position in IVF after many inserts
Embedding drift occurs when similar items receive increasingly dissimilar vectors due to model overfitting
questions.expl: If you change your embedding model, all old embeddings become incompatible — they live in a different vector space. You must either re-embed everything (expensive) or maintain multiple indexes during the transition.

questions.q: The article says 'vector databases are not transactional databases.' What does this mean in practice?
opts: Vector databases cannot run on the same machine as transactional databases
Your authoritative data should live in a primary database; the vector DB is an index for similarity search, not the source of truth
Vector databases support transactions but only for up to 100 vectors at a time
Vector databases must be rebuilt from scratch after any failed transaction
questions.expl: Vector databases are optimized for similarity search, not general-purpose data management. Keep authoritative data in a traditional database; use the vector DB as a search index. They lack ACID guarantees and complex query support.

questions.q: What is the 'cold start' problem specific to vector-based personalization systems?
opts: Index build time is slow when starting from zero vectors
New users have no behavior to embed, so there's no vector to use for finding similar users or items — fallback strategies are needed
Cold environments cause floating point precision errors in similarity computations
The first query after server startup is slow because the index must be loaded into RAM
questions.expl: If you personalize by embedding user behavior, new users have no behavior. There's nothing to embed, so you can't find similar users or recommend based on their taste. You need explicit fallback strategies for new users.
